content: Severe forms of extrapulmonary tuberculosis (TB) include miliary TB or TB meningitis. In children under 15 years of age, extrapulmonary TB forms other than lymphadenopathy (e.g., peripheral nodes or isolated mediastinal masses without compression) are classified as severe. A shorter treatment regimen for multidrug-resistant or rifampin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) typically lasts 9–12 months. This regimen is largely standardized and based on evidence from various settings. The World Health Organization (WHO) has provided guidelines and frameworks for implementing TB diagnostics and treatment strategies, including updates on drug-resistant TB management. The evolution of WHO guidelines for drug-resistant TB treatment includes significant milestones. In 1997, the first guidelines for managing drug-resistant TB were introduced. By 2006, recommendations for incorporating MDR-TB management into national TB control plans were established, with an 18-month standardized regimen. Subsequent updates in 2008 and 2011 included rapid drug susceptibility testing (DST) and revised treatment categories, recommending 4–5 drugs for 20 months, with an 8-month intensive phase. In 2016, a shorter 9–12 month regimen was recommended under programmatic monitoring. By 2019, WHO consolidated guidelines emphasized all-oral regimens, and further updates in 2020 and 2022 included recommendations for bedaquiline (Bdq)-containing regimens and other novel treatment strategies. The 2020 WHO guidelines introduced revised definitions for treatment outcomes, including cured, treatment completed, treatment failed, died, lost to follow-up, and not evaluated. Treatment success is defined as the sum of cured and treatment-completed cases. Sustained treatment success is assessed at 6 months (for drug-resistant and drug-susceptible TB) and 12 months (for drug-resistant TB only) post-treatment, ensuring the patient remains alive and TB-free. The South African TB program treats approximately 10,000 MDR/RR-TB patients annually. Data from 2017 and 2019 cohorts highlight the transition from injectable-based regimens to oral regimens incorporating bedaquiline and linezolid. The 2019 regimen replaced ethionamide with linezolid due to high resistance rates. Exclusion criteria include prior second-line drug treatment, complicated extrapulmonary TB (e.g., meningitis), extensive disease, or resistance to key drugs like bedaquiline or linezolid. The shorter South African 2019 regimen includes a 4–6 month intensive phase with bedaquiline, linezolid, levofloxacin, clofazimine, high-dose isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by a 5-month continuation phase. For children aged 6–12 years, delamanid replaces bedaquiline. The regimen's effectiveness and safety are supported by data, although challenges such as adverse events and acquired resistance remain. WHO's consolidated guidelines emphasize the importance of individualized treatment for complex cases, including pre-XDR and XDR-TB. The guidelines also stress the need for robust monitoring, including drug susceptibility testing and adverse event reporting, to optimize treatment outcomes.
